transcript.text: Sometimes when I open the dishwasher there's grey smelly water in the bottom even though it finished draining fine. Not every day though. Kitchen sink was replaced last month if that matters.

This is a very common issue, and the fact that your kitchen sink was replaced last month is almost certainly the key clue. Even though the dishwasher drains "fine" (meaning it empties during the cycle), grey, smelly water remaining at the bottom usually points to one of three specific problems related to recent plumbing work or general maintenance.

Here’s a breakdown of what’s likely happening and how to fix it:

### 1. The Most Likely Culprit: A Clogged or Improperly Installed Air Gap
If your kitchen sink has an air gap (the small chrome cylinder on the countertop near the faucet), this is the #1 suspect.
• Why it happens: Food debris, grease, or even a small piece of plastic from the sink installation can clog the air gap’s internal passages. When the dishwasher finishes draining, water flows out, but some gets trapped behind the clog and sits in the bottom of the tub until you open it next time.
• The smell: Stagnant water + food particles = grey sludge and a foul odor.
• How to check/fix:
• Remove the chrome cap of the air gap.
• Look inside for debris. Clean it out thoroughly with a toothpick or small brush.
• Run hot water through it to ensure it flows freely.

### 2. The Drain Hose Loop (High Loop) Was Not Installed Correctly
During sink replacements, plumbers sometimes disconnect the dishwasher drain hose and may not reconnect it properly.
• Why it happens: Dishwashers need a "high loop" where the drain hose is clipped up to the underside of the countertop or the sink cabinet before going down into the garbage disposal or sink drain. This prevents dirty sink water from siphoning back into the dishwasher after the cycle ends.
• If missing/low: Water from the sink (which may have been used for washing dishes) can flow backward into the dishwasher while it’s sitting idle, especially if there’s a clog in the sink drain.
• How to check: Look under your sink at the dishwasher drain hose. It should rise up high before dropping down into the disposal or drain pipe. If it sags directly into the drain, clip it higher (use a zip tie or hook).

### 3. Clogged Dishwasher Filter or Drain Pump
Even with recent sink work, your dishwasher filter may be dirty.
• Why it happens: Food particles get trapped in the filter at the bottom of the dishwasher. If not cleaned regularly, they decompose into grey sludge and cause odors. Water can also pool around a clogged pump impeller.
• How to check/fix:
• Remove the bottom rack.
• Twist out the cylindrical or flat filter assembly at the base.
• Rinse it under hot water with dish soap, using a soft brush to remove grease and debris.
• Check the drain area for any visible obstructions (like glass shards or plastic).

### 4. Garbage Disposal Connection Issue
If your dishwasher drains into a garbage disposal:
• Why it happens: The knockout plug inside the disposal’s dishwasher inlet may not have been fully removed during installation, or food has built up in that connection point. This causes slow draining and residual water.
• How to check: Run the disposal for 30 seconds after running the dishwasher. If water backs up into the sink or doesn’t drain quickly, there’s a blockage at the disposal inlet.

---

### ✅ Recommended Action Plan:
1. Clean the filter inside the dishwasher (this is easy and often solves odor issues).
2. Check/clean the air gap on your countertop (if you have one).
3. Inspect the drain hose loop under the sink to ensure it’s high enough.
4. Run a cleaning cycle: Place a cup of white vinegar in the top rack and run a hot water cycle (no dishes) to help dissolve grease and odors. Alternatively, use a dishwasher cleaner tablet.

If these steps don’t resolve it, the issue may be a partial clog in the drain line between the dishwasher and the sink/disposal, which might require professional inspection—especially since recent plumbing work was involved.

I checked under the sink. Since the new sink went in, the dishwasher hose just lies on the cupboard floor and goes straight into the waste spigot, with no high loop. The filter is clean. I'm not sure what an air gap is or whether I have one. Should I loop the hose up?

Yes, you absolutely should create a high loop! That "straight line" from the dishwasher to the waste spigot is exactly why you're getting grey water back in your machine.

### Why This Happens (The Siphon Effect)
When the dishwasher finishes its cycle, it empties out completely. However, because the hose lies flat on the floor and drops straight down into the sink's drain pipe, gravity can cause dirty water from the sink to flow backward up the hose and into your clean dishwasher. This is called back-siphoning.

The "high loop" acts as a barrier. By lifting the hose high up before it goes down, you ensure that even if there’s standing water in the sink drain, it can’t climb back up over the peak of the loop to reach the dishwasher.

### How to Create a High Loop
You don't need special tools for this. Here is how to do it:

1.  Locate the Hose: Find the dishwasher hose where it comes out of the bottom of your machine and runs under the sink.
2.  Find a Mounting Point: Look at the underside of your countertop or the side of the cabinet wall near the sink. You need a place that is as high up as possible (ideally near the top of the cabinet).
3.  Secure the Hose: Use a sturdy clamp, a zip tie, or a dedicated hose clip to attach the middle section of the dishwasher hose to that high point.
• Tip: Make sure you don't kink or crush the hose when you pull it up. It needs to remain open for water to flow through.
4.  Check the Connection: Ensure the end of the hose still connects securely to the waste spigot (the black plastic outlet on your sink drain).

### What About That "Air Gap"?
Since you aren't sure if you have one, here’s how to tell:
• Look at your countertop near the kitchen faucet. Is there a small chrome cylinder with two holes in it? If yes, that is an air gap.
• If you don’t see it: You likely rely on the high loop (which we just discussed) or a "chemical loop" (a specific type of drain connection).

Important Note: If your sink does have an air gap, the dishwasher hose connects to the bottom of that chrome cylinder. In this case, you still need the high loop under the sink, but you also need to make sure the air gap itself isn't clogged (as mentioned in the previous step).

### Next Steps
1.  Create the high loop as described above. This is the most critical fix for your current issue.
2.  Run a cycle: After securing the hose, run an empty dishwasher cycle to see if it drains properly and doesn't leave standing water.
3.  Check the garbage disposal (if you have one): If your sink drain connects to a garbage disposal, make sure the small plastic knock-out plug inside the disposal's inlet was removed during installation. If this plug is still in place, nothing can drain from the dishwasher into the disposal!

By creating that high loop, you should see an immediate improvement and stop the grey water from returning.
